F057.why: The policy is a ban with exceptions only in approved cases (ACC COSC 1336 'Exceptions to this policy will only be made under specific circumstances approved by the'; CSIS 4355 'exceptions will be made on a case-by-case basis'), which is AI allowed only under a stated limit, not a general permission.

F058.value: Never use AI to give students feedback on their assessments.
F058.why: The only statement (Vermont CS 2510 'I guarantee that I will never use AI to' provide feedback on any assessments) is about feedback on assessments, not grading as such.

F059.value: Instructors should never use AI to give students feedback on assessments.
F059.why: Same single Vermont CS 2510 statement names feedback on assessments, so the grading label misstates it.

F060.value: If you detect what you think is AI-generated work, you may talk with the student about it, file an integrity charge, or both.
F060.why: Wellesley CS 111 'we may, at any point in the semester, have a' conversation 'and/or file an Honor Code charge' sets no order, so 'before any report' adds a detail.

F061.value: Instructors may talk with the student about suspected AI misuse, report it, or both.
F061.why: Same Wellesley CS 111 'and/or' wording gives conversation and charge as alternatives or both, not conversation first.

F062.why: The student's act is not using AI while doing the work (Grinnell CSC 213 'prohibited for all work in this course'; Wright State 'for any work for this section'); course-start is the instructor's act of telling the rules, which no statement asks of students.

F063.why: The encouraged use happens while doing the work (Georgia Tech CS 1301 'when working on exercises'; Vanderbilt CS 4260 'to design, implement, document, and evaluate your programming assignments'; Stony Brook 'throughout this course, including on the project').

F064.why: AI is allowed but only in one form (Berkeley CS 61B 'must take place exclusively through browser-based chatbots'; Cornell CS 1110 'limit such work to a chat interface'), which is a stated limit rather than a ban on AI.

F065.value: You must not use agentic AI coding tools; where AI is allowed, use it only through a chat interface.
F065.why: Three of four statements ban agentic tools (Berkeley 'agentic coding tools are outright banned', Cornell 'refrain from agentic tools', Princeton 'Using agentic AI'), a point the chat-only directive misses.

F066.value: You must not use generative AI, because it would remove the learning benefit of the work.
F066.why: USC CSCI 103L 'Because use of generative AI would remove any of that benefit, we do not allow its use' does not name homework, so 'on homework' adds scope.

F067.why: Most statements are rules for keeping and submitting complete logs (NC State CSC 316 'must not be edited or truncated'; UIUC CS 128 'Never ask the AI to reproduce the conversation' and 'complete and unaltered record'), not detection or sanctions; only Princeton ties it to evidence of a violation.

F068.value: You should use only the packages, classes and methods the course has listed or covered in class.
F068.why: Neither statement mentions AI suggestions (Colby CS 343 'only use Python packages listed in Software'; Dartmouth COSC 10 'classes or methods that we have not discussed in class').

F069.value: Students should use only the packages, classes and methods the course has listed or covered.
F069.why: The statements are about allowed packages and classes (Colby CS 343, Dartmouth COSC 10), not lines of AI code or AI-written solutions, so the policy is misfiled.

F070.why: Colby CS 151 'You cannot receive extension points without an AI usage statement' requires a statement and lists no allowed uses.

F071.why: Colby CS 151 sets what earns points when work is graded ('cannot receive extension points').

F072.why: Columbia COMS W4118 'links to logs are not accepted' sets the form of a required log, not which AI uses are allowed.

F073.value: Students may use AI freely outside graded work and for code they do not submit.
F073.why: The freedom is outside graded coursework (CCSF CS 110B 'Outside of class assignments and exams'; Cornell CS 1110 'for code that you do not submit'; USF CS 326 'Outside a session'), so 'on coursework' misstates it.

F074.value: You may use AI only for the limited uses your course lists, such as learning, debugging, projects or open-format homework.
F074.why: Only Vermont CS 1210 adds '(with citation)'; the rest list allowed uses without it (Bucknell 'Allowed: Learning, debugging, projects'; LMU 'limit the use of GenAI ... to the following cases').

F075.why: The statements grant an option (Harvey Mudd 'You may use LLMs'; Penn 'you are welcome to use AI'; LMU lists 'Interpreting error messages' as an allowed case).

F076.value: Students may use AI to explain error messages.
F076.why: No statement says students must find bugs themselves and only UW CSE 123 forbids fixes; the rest permit explanation (Harvey Mudd, LMU x5, Michigan, Penn, UIUC, UW CSE 351).

F077.value: You may use AI to interpret or explain error messages.
F077.why: Only UW CSE 123 adds '(but not to provide a fix)', and Michigan EECS 280 even allows 'getting suggestions for debugging a problem'.

F078.why: All six statements permit a use (LMU x5 'Generating short documentation strings and type hints'; UCSC 'may be used for code comments').

F079.value: You may use AI to generate short docstrings, type hints, comments and other documentation, citing it where your course requires.
F079.why: Citation is a condition in UCSC CSE 30 only ('if properly cited'); the five LMU statements give no citation condition and say 'short'.

F080.value: Students may use AI to write documentation such as docstrings, type hints and comments.
F080.why: No statement mentions rewriting AI code examples; all permit AI-written documentation (LMU 'Generating short documentation strings'; UCSC 'code comments, explanations, and other documentation').

F081.why: The use is tied to graded work after it is assessed (Michigan EECS 376 'after the deadline has passed'; 'whether it thinks your graded solution should earn more points on our rubric'), not to reviewing policy over time.

F082.why: UT Austin CS 314 'You may use generative AIs to help understand why' graded tests failed concerns assessed work after the deadline, not policy review, matching its sibling CT10.c04.

F083.why: The statements promote staff help, not AI use (Pomona 'primary resource ... rather than AI tools'; USC 'we prefer you just get help from course staff'; Brown 'we recommend you ask a TA').

F084.why: The statements invite feedback about AI, not AI use (Tufts 'we would love to hear any honest feedback'; Wellesley 'bring to our attention any biases that you see').

F085.why: The policy asks for reflection when AI is used, not more AI use, and NC State CSC 316 makes it required ('Each conversation/session must include a brief reflection'); CSC 216 'Reflect on the use of AI tools'.

F086.value: You must name the AI tool you used in your disclosure or citation.
F086.why: Only NJIT CS 332 asks for 'the AI tool and version'; the others ask only for the tool (Memphis 'The name of the tool used') or a description.

F087.value: You must cite the AI tool and the prompt you gave it, and mark where its code appears.
F087.why: Only UCSD CSE 110 asks for version in comments; tool, prompt and marking recur across Clemson ('the AI app and the specification'), UMass Boston ('marking START, citing the prompt'), ODU ('indicate where code has been directly quoted').

F088.value: You must cite AI code when it is nontrivial.
F088.why: LMU 'cite the usage if the code you utilize is nontrivial' sets a threshold, not a limit on citing trivial code.

F089.why: Wellesley CS 111 'required to read an AI academic paper and present it' requires reading about AI, not AI use, and takes no position on AI use.

F090.value: You must not use AI to analyze data, draw conclusions from experiments or data analysis, or interpret simulation results.
F090.why: Neither Rowan statement says 'in graded work' ('Analyzing data, drawing conclusions...'; 'interpret, process, or analyze results from simulations').

F091.why: The rule is about crediting AI as an author, not about using AI (MIT 'should never be listed as a co-author'; NC State 'no LLM tool should be credited as co-author'), and several statements are neutral reasons (Louisville, Seattle, Florida).

F092.why: The policy asks an act (not crediting AI) when writing up work (NC State 'credited as co-author on a research paper'; Saint Louis 'authorship must reflect substantive human contributions'), so it is not just background.

F093.why: The student gets approval before using AI in their own thesis or research (Alabama Huntsville 'prior to using these tools'; UNC Charlotte 'prior approval from their faculty mentor for the project'), which is part of doing the work, not course design or institutional set-up.

F094.why: The advisor or committee decides (CSULB 'consult their thesis advisors whether any usage of AI tools is allowed'; UTHSC 'will decide on the use of AI tools'; Utah 'at the discretion of the student's supervisory'; Yeshiva 'unless the supervisor states otherwise').

F095.why: The default governs how the student's AI use is treated while doing the work (UNC Greensboro 'will be treated analogously to assistance from another person'); course-start is the instructor's telling of rules, which these statements do not ask of students.

F096.why: Vanderbilt 'the use of such tools is permitted but must be disclosed' is a default for using and disclosing AI while doing the work, not a start-of-course act by the student.

F097.why: Understanding what you submit is a duty whatever the AI rule (Clemson 'The work must reflect the student's understanding'; Kansas 'expected to understand the code that you submit'; UCSC 'fully understood by you').

F098.why: Two of three are integrity or responsibility statements with no position on AI use (Berkeley 'I act with honesty, integrity'; Yeshiva 'take responsibility for the accuracy and originality').

F099.why: Ohio 'you must be wary of unintentional plagiarism or fabrication of data' is a duty of care that sets no limit on AI use.

F100.value: Avoid entering assignment or exam answers into generative AI tools.
F100.why: UNLV says only that entering answers 'is not advisable', which is advice, so 'Do not' overstates the force.

F101.why: The student's act is citing or disclosing AI in submitted work (Austin CC 'Submitting AI-generated content as your own without disclosure'; Old Dominion 'may not include AI-generated content in your final submission without attribution'); the statements define the offence rather than detection or sanctions.

F102.why: This is a verify-output duty that grants no permission (Georgetown 'Run your code and check any output'; Clemson 'Assume generated code may be insecure or incorrect'; UAB 'your responsibility to identify errors').

F103.why: Checking AI-given citations is a verify-output duty with no position on AI use (Arkansas 'existence of AI-generated references should be confirmed'; Tulane 'Verify every citation'; NYU 'Do the citations listed exist?').

F104.value: You may use AI to explain code syntax or specific code snippets and to provide examples.
F104.why: Both statements are options (BYU 'AI can be used to help understand code syntax'; RIT 'Asking it to explain a specific snippet'), and the directive read as an instruction.

F105.value: Disclosure of AI use may be optional for minor uses such as grammar checking, brainstorming, or suggesting how to organize a paper or a title.
F105.why: No statement mentions finding references; Princeton names 'grammar checkers' and Oregon State 'Brainstorm or suggest how to organize a paper, or suggest a paper or section title'.

F106.value: You may use AI for data analysis if your use complies with transparency policies.
F106.why: UPR Rio Piedras 'será permitido, siempre que cumpla con las políticas de transparencia' gives only the transparency condition, nothing about oversight.

F107.value: You may use AI to summarize sources for your own understanding, but not to summarize assigned readings unless your instructor permits it.
F107.why: Three statements allow summarizing outright (Jackson State, South Alabama, Berkeley) while three limit it for assigned readings (LSU New Orleans 'Summarizing assigned course readings unless explicitly permitted'; UNC 'Unless I specifically allow it'; UTHealth 'not primarily assigned'), so the limit belongs in the directive as a second-person rule, not as 'some policies'.

F108.why: The use is studying and practice outside graded work (Clemson 'Generating practice questions to study'; UW 'ungraded practice exercise'; Embry-Riddle 'non-graded examples').

F109.why: The statements advise thinking first whatever the AI rule and grant nothing (GWU 'engage in your own independent thinking before seeking support'; South Dakota 'Start with your own ideas'; Kansas 'Try to do the assignment first').

F110.why: Prompt-writing advice takes no position on whether to use AI (San Diego State 'Opt for clear and explicit phrasing'; Santa Clara 'Provide context to questions'; South Dakota 'Ask specific questions').

F111.why: The statements advise refining prompts, not using AI (Michigan-Dearborn 'expect to revise prompts'; UIC 'Continuously test and refine your prompts'; Vermont 'Don't expect it to produce its best result on a first try').

F112.why: A security duty with no position on AI use (UTHealth 'must use VPN while accessing the MSBMI AIChat off-campus'; UTSA 'enable this option to add an extra layer of security').

F113.value: Consider creating and maintaining an AI portfolio throughout your time at the university.
F113.why: UCF 'consider creating and maintaining an AI Portfolio' is a suggestion to students; the instructor clause comes from Montana 'refine your teaching methods', which does not address students.

F114.value: students for the UCF statement; move The University of Montana statement to an instructor policy
F114.why: Montana 'Continuously evaluate and refine your teaching methods' addresses instructors, while UCF addresses students.

F115.why: Swarthmore 'Confirm what's acceptable before using genAI tools for resumes' is a student check before a use, not course design or institutional set-up.

F116.why: UAB and UNT 'AI generated submissions cannot achieve a passing grade' set what counts when work is graded.

F117.value: In some courses part of your grade evaluates your documentation of AI use, and AI use can make it harder for your instructor to evaluate your work.
F117.why: Only UAB grades AI documentation ('A portion of your term grade will evaluate your documentation of AI use'); Florida 'would make it harder to evaluate your work' and CU Denver are general, so the directive overstates grading as universal.
